# heatmap of a covariance or correlation matrix (row 1 at the top)
show_matrix <- function(M, main = "", zlim = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(M))) {
  n <- nrow(M)
  pal <- colorRampPalette(c("firebrick", "white", "steelblue"))(101)
  par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

}

Packages: `mvtnorm`, `lme4`, `nlme`, `glmmTMB`, `cmdstanr`, `posterior`,
`brms`. The reference handout
[*Mixed models in R: nlme, lme4, and glmmTMB*](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf)
compares the three mixed-model packages' syntax and says when to use
each.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
Chapter 10, sections 10.3-10.6 (pp. 423-441).

# Autocorrelation and mixed models in R {#mixed-models-r}

To fit a likelihood with correlated observations, we need a covariance 
matrix $V$ to capture that correlation structure!

Here we start by modeling data that is correlated through time. Then we 
walk through some reasons why structured-variance models are harder to fit than the independent models from earlier in the course (oh, if it were only as simple as summing up log-likelihoods across all observations!!). Then we will fit random intercept and
random slope models with some popular R packages, checking them against
hand-written likelihood functions where we can (it's not always possible!).

As we saw last time, when observations aren't independent, 
the noise part (multivariate normal is 
by far the most common distribution for correlated errors)
is described with a structured covariance matrix $V$ (see
[modeling variance](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#variance)). 
We saw last week that a standard
[random intercept model](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept)
makes $V$ block-diagonal: observations in the same group are correlated (share a
non-zero covariance), while other observations are independent.

The next two things we'll look at are (1) correlation that fades away with time (autoregressive models), and
(2) discrete/categorical groups that differ in both their mean response (intercept) and the effect of a predictor (i.e., how much do groups differ in *how they respond* to the predictor?). These are often called 'random slope' models. 

We'll continue using the simulated pinyon ring widths
from [week 11](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#lm-likelihood):
5 trees in each of 4 stands, 1996-2020, averaged into one chronology per
stand.

```{r pinyon-data}
# pinyon ring widths (mm): 4 stands x 5 trees x 25 years; simulated
library(mvtnorm)
set.seed(21)
years <- 1996:2020
n_yr <- length(years)
precip <- round(rgamma(n_yr, shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1)   # winter precipitation (cm)
stand_eff <- rnorm(4, 0, 0.12)
ar_dev <- matrix(0, 4, n_yr)            # shared year-to-year deviations within each stand
for (j in 1:4) {
  ar_dev[j, 1] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.08 / sqrt(1 - 0.6^2))
  for (t in 2:n_yr) ar_dev[j, t] <- 0.6 * ar_dev[j, t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.08)
}
rings <- expand.grid(year = years, tree = 1:5, stand = LETTERS[1:4])
rings$tree_id <- paste0(rings$stand, rings$tree)
tree_eff <- setNames(rnorm(20, 0, 0.1), unique(rings$tree_id))
j <- match(rings$stand, LETTERS)
t <- match(rings$year, years)
rings$precip <- precip[t]
rings$width <- round(0.35 + stand_eff[j] + tree_eff[rings$tree_id] + 0.025 * rings$precip +
                       ar_dev[cbind(j, t)] + rnorm(nrow(rings), 0, 0.1), 2)

chron <- aggregate(width ~ stand + year + precip, data = rings, FUN = mean)
chron <- chron[order(chron$stand, chron$year), ]
chron$stand <- factor(chron$stand)
tree_means <- aggregate(width ~ stand + tree_id, data = rings, FUN = mean)
```

## 1. Autocorrelation: AR(1) {#ar1}

Let's take this chronology over 25 years (from stand A) and ask:
is growth declining linearly over time, after accounting for precipitation? 

If we regress ring width on precipitation and year, and look at the residuals:

```{r ar1-resid, fig.width=7, fig.height=8.5}
chron_a <- chron[chron$stand == "A", ]
chron_a$year_c <- chron_a$year - 2008          # centered year: 0 = 2008
fit_lm_a <- lm(width ~ precip + year_c, data = chron_a)
summary(fit_lm_a)$coefficients
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4.5, 2, 1))
plot(chron_a$year, chron_a$width, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Mean ring width (mm)", main = "Stand A chronology")
trend <- predict(fit_lm_a, newdata = data.frame(precip = mean(chron_a$precip),
                                                year_c = chron_a$year_c))
lines(chron_a$year, trend, lwd = 2, col = "red")   # year trend at mean precipitation
plot(chron_a$year, resid(fit_lm_a), type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Residual", main = "Residuals from lm()")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
acf(resid(fit_lm_a), lag.max = 10, main = "")
title("Autocorrelation of the residuals", line = 0.8)
```

The `acf()` panel shows the correlation between residuals $k$ years
apart. The lag-1 value, `r f2(acf(resid(fit_lm_a), plot = FALSE)$acf[2])`,
falls inside the dashed bounds, so (surprisingly) this plot can't rule out
independence even though we KNOW there is fairly strong autocorrelation 
(we simulated it that way). With 25 years the bounds are wide
($\pm 1.96/\sqrt{25} \approx \pm 0.39$), and a series this short often
hides autocorrelation that's really there.

Other evidence helps. For example, the correlation decays down to zero- 
a classic sign of serially correlated errors. Also, lag-1 residual correlation 
is positive in all four stands:

```{r ar1-lag1-stands}
lag1 <- function(dat) {
  dat$year_c <- dat$year - 2008
  acf(resid(lm(width ~ precip + year_c, data = dat)), plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
}
round(sapply(split(chron, chron$stand), lag1), 2)
```

and it's realistic just based on common sense: stored carbohydrates and
needles that live several years can lead to year effects (e.g., a good growth year) bleeding into the next year(s).

The simplest model for temporally correlated errors is the **first-order autoregressive** model, AR(1): each year's total "error" is a fraction $\rho$ of last year's plus
new noise (often called an 'innovation'),

$$\eta_t = \rho\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2), \qquad |\rho| < 1$$

Here $\eta_t$ is the autocorrelated error and $\varepsilon_t$ is
independent noise. Note: many time-series texts
(and `nlme`'s output) call the coefficient $\phi$ rather than $\rho$.

Taking variances of both sides, with $\eta_{t-1}$ and $\varepsilon_t$
independent and $\text{Var}(\eta_t) = \text{Var}(\eta_{t-1})$ (a
stationary series):

$$\text{Var}(\eta_t) = \rho^2\text{Var}(\eta_t) + \sigma^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{Var}(\eta_t) = \frac{\sigma^2}{1 - \rho^2}$$

and the correlation between deviations $k$ steps apart is $\rho^k$
(Bolker eq. 10.3.7). So the covariance between years $s$ and $t$ is

$$V_{st} = \frac{\sigma^2}{1 - \rho^2}\,\rho^{|s - t|}$$

The `abs(row(M) - col(M))` trick from Bolker (p. 427) builds the matrix
of lags:

```{r ar1-matrix}
lags <- abs(outer(1:25, 1:25, "-"))
V_ar1 <- function(rho, sigma) sigma^2 / (1 - rho^2) * rho^lags
round(V_ar1(0.6, 0.08)[1:5, 1:5], 4)
```

Fitting needs $|\rho| < 1$, so we optimize $\text{atanh}(\rho)$, which
can be any number (unbounded), and convert back with `tanh()` 
(which converts any unbounded real number to a bounded real number between -1 and 1. 

Standard errors from the Hessian are then on the atanh (correlation) and log (variance) scales; 
if you'd like, you can use the delta method to put them back into the natural scale for $\rho$ and $\sigma$ (see the reference handout
[*The Delta Method*](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_DeltaMethod.pdf)).

```{r ar1-fit}
# mean: a + b * precip + c * year_c; AR(1) errors with rho = tanh(par[4]), sigma = exp(par[5])
nll_ar1 <- function(par) {
  mu <- par[1] + par[2] * chron_a$precip + par[3] * chron_a$year_c
  V <- V_ar1(tanh(par[4]), exp(par[5]))
  -dmvnorm(chron_a$width, mu, V, log = TRUE)
}
fit_ar1 <- optim(c(coef(fit_lm_a), 0, log(0.1)), nll_ar1, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
c(a = fit_ar1$par[1], b = fit_ar1$par[2], c = fit_ar1$par[3],
  rho = tanh(fit_ar1$par[4]), sigma = exp(fit_ar1$par[5]))

library(nlme)
fit_gls <- gls(width ~ precip + year_c, data = chron_a,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ year), method = "ML")
coef(fit_gls)
coef(fit_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)   # rho (nlme calls it Phi)
```

```{r ar1-se, echo=FALSE}
trend_ind <- summary(fit_lm_a)$coefficients["year_c", ]
se_ar1 <- sqrt(diag(solve(fit_ar1$hessian)))[3]
p_ar1 <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(fit_ar1$par[3] / se_ar1))
rho_hat <- tanh(fit_ar1$par[4])
se_precip <- c(summary(fit_lm_a)$coefficients["precip", 2], sqrt(diag(solve(fit_ar1$hessian)))[2])
```

The estimated $\rho$ is `r f2(rho_hat)`. The trend estimate barely
moves, but its standard error grows:

- assuming independence: `r f4(trend_ind[1])` mm/yr, SE `r f4(trend_ind[2])`,
  $p =$ `r f3(trend_ind[4])`;
- with AR(1) errors: `r f4(fit_ar1$par[3])` mm/yr, SE `r f4(se_ar1)`
  (from the Hessian), $p =$ `r f2(p_ar1)`.

The simulation has no trend at all.

The [mixed models handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf)
shows the same AR(1) fit in `glmmTMB`, along with other residual
structures (spatial correlation, unequal variances).

The widget below builds two covariance structures for 12 observations
and simulates data from them. The heatmap shows correlations (blue
positive, red negative).

```{r widget-cov, echo=FALSE}
widget("cov_structures.html")
```

> **Question:** With $\rho$ near 0.9, what does a single AR(1) series look
> like? How could you tell it apart from a slow trend?

## 2. Why these models are harder to fit {#harder}

The AR(1) model above and the
[random intercept](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept)
model for the 20 tree means were both fit with the same `optim()` method we've been using for independent-likelihood functions. The difference is that the NLL is NOT
computed as a sum of (negative) log-likelihoods. Instead we've used the multivariate
normal density function to compute the likelihood in one fell swoop!

```{r ri-refit}
y_tree <- tree_means$width
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + stand, data = tree_means)
V_ri <- function(sigma_b, sigma) sigma_b^2 * Z %*% t(Z) + sigma^2 * diag(20)
nll_ri <- function(par) -dmvnorm(y_tree, rep(par[1], 20), V_ri(exp(par[2]), exp(par[3])), log = TRUE)
fit_ri <- optim(c(mean(y_tree), log(0.1), log(0.1)), nll_ri, method = "BFGS")
sb_hat <- exp(fit_ri$par[2])
s_hat <- exp(fit_ri$par[3])
c(mu = fit_ri$par[1], sigma_b = sb_hat, sigma = s_hat)
```

Three things make structured-variance models harder than their
independent cousins.

**Each NLL evaluation costs more.** Under independence the NLL is a sum
of $n$ terms. The MVN needs the determinant and inverse of an
$n \times n$ matrix (in practice a Cholesky factorization), which takes
on the order of $n^3$ operations. Doubling the data multiplies the time
per evaluation by about 8, and `optim()` evaluates the NLL hundreds of
times.

```{r timing, cache=TRUE}
# milliseconds per NLL evaluation, averaged over 'reps' evaluations
time_nll <- function(n, reps = 10) {
  y <- rnorm(n)
  V <- 0.5^abs(outer(1:n, 1:n, "-"))
  ms <- function(expr) 1000 * system.time(for (i in 1:reps) expr)[["elapsed"]] / reps
  c(n = n, independent = ms(sum(dnorm(y, 0, 1, log = TRUE))),
    mvn = ms(dmvnorm(y, rep(0, n), V, log = TRUE)))
}
set.seed(1)
timings <- t(sapply(c(250, 500, 1000, 2000), time_nll))
timings
```

With 2000 observations, one MVN evaluation took about
`r round(timings[4, "mvn"])` ms here; the independent NLL took a small
fraction of a millisecond. An `optim()` run needing 300 evaluations
would take about `r round(300 * timings[4, "mvn"] / 60000, 1)` minutes,
against well under a second. (Packages like `lme4` and `nlme` exploit
the structure of $V$, such as its blocks, to avoid most of this cost.)

**The likelihood surface is awkward.** Below are NLL contours for the
two models, with the other parameters set to their best values at each
point (a profile). The shaded region is within 1.92 NLL units of the
minimum, an approximate 95% confidence region.

```{r surfaces, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, cache=TRUE}
# profile out the mean parameters by generalized least squares at each (variance) grid point
gls_nll <- function(y, X, V) {
  Vi <- solve(V)
  b <- solve(t(X) %*% Vi %*% X, t(X) %*% Vi %*% y)
  -dmvnorm(y, as.vector(X %*% b), V, log = TRUE)
}
sb_grid <- seq(0.002, 0.45, length.out = 70)
s_grid <- seq(0.04, 0.16, length.out = 70)
X1 <- matrix(1, 20, 1)
nll_grid_ri <- outer(sb_grid, s_grid, Vectorize(function(a, b) gls_nll(y_tree, X1, V_ri(a, b))))
# AR(1): fix rho and the trend c; profile out a, b (GLS) and sigma (closed form)
prof_ar1 <- function(rho, c_trend) {
  R <- rho^lags / (1 - rho^2)
  y <- chron_a$width - c_trend * chron_a$year_c
  Xp <- cbind(1, chron_a$precip)
  Ri <- solve(R)
  b <- solve(t(Xp) %*% Ri %*% Xp, t(Xp) %*% Ri %*% y)
  r <- as.vector(y - Xp %*% b)
  s2 <- as.numeric(t(r) %*% Ri %*% r) / 25
  -dmvnorm(r, rep(0, 25), s2 * R, log = TRUE)
}
rho_grid <- seq(-0.5, 0.95, length.out = 70)
c_grid <- seq(-0.02, 0.01, length.out = 70)
nll_grid_ar <- outer(rho_grid, c_grid, Vectorize(prof_ar1))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
draw_surface <- function(x, y, z, xlab, ylab, main, best) {
  z <- z - min(z)
  image(x, y, z <= 1.92, col = c("white", "lightskyblue1"), xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = main)
  contour(x, y, z, levels = c(0.5, 1, 1.92, 3, 5, 10, 20), add = TRUE, col = "grey30")
  points(best[1], best[2], pch = 3, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
  box()
}
draw_surface(sb_grid, s_grid, nll_grid_ri, expression(sigma[b] ~ "(among stands)"),
             expression(sigma ~ "(among trees)"), "Random intercept, 4 stands",
             c(sb_hat, s_hat))
draw_surface(rho_grid, c_grid, nll_grid_ar, expression(rho),
             "Trend (mm/yr)", "AR(1) with a trend, stand A", c(rho_hat, fit_ar1$par[3]))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

```{r surface-ranges, echo=FALSE}
in_ri <- (nll_grid_ri - min(nll_grid_ri)) <= 1.92
sb_range <- range(sb_grid[apply(in_ri, 1, any)])
in_ar <- (nll_grid_ar - min(nll_grid_ar)) <= 1.92
trend_at <- function(r) range(c_grid[in_ar[which.min(abs(rho_grid - r)), ]])
trend_0 <- trend_at(0)
trend_hat <- trend_at(rho_hat)
```

- **Random intercept:** the region runs from about
  $\sigma_b =$ `r f2(sb_range[1])` to `r f2(sb_range[2])`, more than a
  fourfold range, while $\sigma$ (from 20 trees) is much better
  determined. Four stands give four draws of $b_j$, so the data say
  little about their spread. With fewer stands or smaller differences
  among them, the region reaches $\sigma_b = 0$; the optimizer may stop
  on that boundary, where the usual Hessian and LRT approximations fail
  (the same problem as in
  [comparing Poisson and negative binomial models](Week10_ModelComparison.html#frequentist)).
- **AR(1) with a trend:** here the axes are $\rho$ and the trend, with
  everything else profiled out. The region is a fan, not an ellipse. Near
  $\rho = 0$ the plausible trends run from about
  `r f4(trend_0[1])` to `r f4(trend_0[2])` mm/yr, all below 0 (dashed
  line). At $\rho =$ `r f2(rho_hat)` they run from `r f4(trend_hat[1])`
  to `r f4(trend_hat[2])`. A slow drift and strong autocorrelation can
  explain the same wandering series, so what we conclude about a mean
  parameter depends on a variance parameter, and the two have to be
  estimated together. A lopsided region like this also makes
  Hessian-based intervals, which assume an ellipse, less trustworthy.

**Parameters must keep $V$ valid.** A variance must be positive,
$|\rho|$ must be below 1, and in general $V$ must stay
[positive definite](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#valid-covariance).
An unconstrained step can leave the allowed region, and `dmvnorm()`
then fails. We avoided this by optimizing $\log\sigma$ and
$\text{atanh}(\rho)$; richer structures need cleverer parameterizations
(for example, building $V$ from its Cholesky factor, as Stan does in
the [Bayesian version](#stan-model)).

None of this is a reason to assume independence when it's false. Specialized software helps a LOT in fitting these models, and Bayesian
methods, which sample the random effects instead of integrating over
them, make it straightforward to build and interpret hierarchical models.

## 3. Random slopes {#random-slopes}

A new question for a bigger data set: **is drought sensitivity the same
everywhere?** Twelve pinyon stands span an elevation gradient. For each
stand we have a ring-width chronology and that stand's winter
precipitation, but the records differ in length: two stands have 30
reliable years, two have only 5. (These data are also simulated.) We
express precipitation in 10-cm units, centered at 20 cm, so the
intercept is the ring width in a 20-cm winter and the slope is the
change in width per extra 10 cm.

```{r drought-data}
set.seed(12)
n_years <- rep(c(30, 24, 18, 12, 8, 5), each = 2)        # record length per stand
tau_true <- c(0.15, 0.10)                                 # among-stand SDs: intercept, slope
rho_true <- -0.6
G_true <- diag(tau_true) %*% matrix(c(1, rho_true, rho_true, 1), 2) %*% diag(tau_true)
ab_true <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)              # each stand's intercept and slope
stand_names <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:12)
drought <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)),
                      year = unlist(lapply(n_years, function(n) seq(2021 - n, 2020))))
j <- as.integer(drought$stand)
drought$precip <- round(rgamma(nrow(drought), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1)
drought$precip10 <- (drought$precip - 20) / 10
drought$width <- round(ab_true[j, 1] + ab_true[j, 2] * drought$precip10 +
                         rnorm(nrow(drought), 0, 0.12), 2)
head(drought)
```

Residuals here are independent (no AR(1) term), so the only correlation
among observations comes from the shared stand effects.

```{r drought-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
nopool <- t(sapply(split(drought, drought$stand), function(s) coef(lm(width ~ precip10, data = s))))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(width ~ precip, data = drought, col = "grey60", pch = 16, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Winter precipitation (cm)", ylab = "Ring width (mm)")
for (s in seq_len(12)) {
  xr <- range(drought$precip10[drought$stand == stand_names[s]])
  lines(20 + 10 * xr, nopool[s, 1] + nopool[s, 2] * xr, lwd = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 1, 2),
        lty = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 2, 1))
}
legend("topleft", c("stand with 12-30 years", "stand with 5-8 years"), lty = 1:2, lwd = 2:1,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
plot(nopool, pch = 19, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)", cex = 1.1, xlim = range(nopool[, 1]) + c(0, 0.05))
text(nopool, labels = stand_names, pos = 4, cex = 0.7, col = "grey40")
```

Left: one least-squares line per stand. Right: each stand's own
intercept and slope. Stands that grow less in an average winter tend to
respond more to precipitation, as you might expect if low-elevation
stands are closer to their water limit.

A **random slope** model lets both the intercept and the slope vary
among stands, and lets them be correlated:

$$\text{width}_{jt} = (\mu_a + a_j) + (\mu_b + b_j)\,x_{jt} + \varepsilon_{jt},
\qquad \varepsilon_{jt} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2)$$

$$\begin{pmatrix} a_j \\ b_j \end{pmatrix} \sim
\text{MVN}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, G\right),
\qquad
G = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_a^2 & \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b \\ \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b & \tau_b^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

where $x_{jt}$ is precipitation (10-cm units, centered) for stand $j$
in year $t$. There are six parameters: two fixed effects ($\mu_a$,
$\mu_b$), the among-stand SDs of the intercepts and slopes ($\tau_a$,
$\tau_b$), their correlation $\rho$, and the residual SD $\sigma$. The
24 stand deviations $a_j, b_j$ are not parameters in this likelihood.
We never observe them, so the likelihood averages over every value they
could take, weighted by how likely each is under their MVN
distribution. This works like the
[law of total probability](Week3_ProbabilityAndBayes.html#conditional),
with an integral in place of the sum. For Normal data the average works
out to another MVN, with the covariance matrix below, so no integral
appears in the code. This step is called *integrating out* the random
effects.

What covariance matrix results? Within stand $j$, write the observations as
$y_j = X_j\mu + Z_j u_j + \varepsilon_j$, with $u_j = (a_j, b_j)^T$ and
$Z_j$ the two-column matrix $[1, x]$ for that stand. Then

$$V_j = Z_j G Z_j^T + \sigma^2 I$$

and $V$ is block diagonal again, one block per stand, but the
covariance between two years in the same stand now depends on how wet
those years were.

These variance rules give $V_j$ whatever the distributions of $u_j$ and
$\varepsilon_j$ (the law of total variance,
$\text{Var}(y) = E[\text{Var}(y \mid u)] + \text{Var}(E[y \mid u])$,
averages over $u$ just as the likelihood does). Only for the MVN are the
mean and covariance the whole distribution, so only there do they give
the likelihood. A Poisson or binomial GLMM needs the integral itself
(see the [GLMM bonus](#glmm-by-hand)).

R's mixed-model packages share a formula syntax for the random part:

```{r formula-table, echo=FALSE}
syntax <- data.frame(
  Formula = c("<code>(1 | stand)</code>", "<code>(precip10 | stand)</code>",
              "<code>(precip10 || stand)</code>", "<code>(1 | stand/tree)</code>",
              "<code>(1 | stand) + (1 | year)</code>"),
  Meaning = c("an intercept for each stand",
              "an intercept and a slope for each stand, correlated (same as <code>(1 + precip10 | stand)</code>)",
              "an intercept and a slope for each stand, uncorrelated",
              "stand intercepts plus tree-within-stand intercepts (nested)",
              "stand intercepts and year intercepts (crossed: every stand is measured in many years)"),
  `Variance parameters` = c("1", "3", "2", "2", "2"),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(syntax, format = "html", escape = FALSE,
             table.attr = "class='table table-condensed'")
```

(`(x || stand)` is shorthand for two separate terms,
`(1 | stand) + (0 + x | stand)`: one for the intercepts and one for the
slopes, each with its own variance and no correlation between them. The
shorthand works as intended only when `x` is numeric; with a factor,
`lme4` still estimates correlations among the factor's levels.) Each formula
adds the residual variance $\sigma^2$ on top. The
[mixed models handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf)
writes each of these in `nlme` and `glmmTMB` syntax too.

## 4. Mixed models in R {#packages}

**`lme4`.** `lmer()` fits Normal mixed models; `glmer()` fits
generalized ones. Here are the random intercept and random slope models
for the drought data:

```{r lmer-fits}
library(lme4)
fit_ri_lmer <- lmer(width ~ precip10 + (1 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
fit_rs_lmer <- lmer(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
fixef(fit_rs_lmer)
VarCorr(fit_rs_lmer)
AIC(fit_ri_lmer, fit_rs_lmer)
```

```{r lmer-numbers, echo=FALSE}
vc_rs <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_rs_lmer))$sdcor
aic_gain <- AIC(fit_ri_lmer) - AIC(fit_rs_lmer)
```

Letting the slopes vary costs two parameters and lowers AIC by
`r round(aic_gain, 1)`. The estimated correlation between stand
intercepts and slopes is `r f2(vc_rs[3])`. (`REML = FALSE` gives the
plain MLE; by default `lmer()` uses REML, which corrects the downward
bias in variance estimates. Use the MLE when comparing models with
different fixed effects by likelihood ratio or AIC.)

**`nlme` and `glmmTMB`.** The same model in two other packages:

```{r other-packages}
fit_rs_lme <- lme(width ~ precip10, random = ~ precip10 | stand, data = drought, method = "ML")

library(glmmTMB)
fit_rs_tmb <- glmmTMB(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought)   # ML by default
```

**By hand.** The likelihood is a product over stands of MVN densities,
one block $V_j$ each. Building $G$ from $\log\tau_a$, $\log\tau_b$, and
$\text{atanh}(\rho)$ keeps it a valid covariance matrix wherever
`optim()` steps:

```{r rs-optim}
rows_by_stand <- split(seq_len(nrow(drought)), drought$stand)
nll_rs <- function(par) {
  tau <- exp(par[3:4])
  rho <- tanh(par[5])
  sigma <- exp(par[6])
  G <- matrix(c(tau[1]^2, rho * tau[1] * tau[2], rho * tau[1] * tau[2], tau[2]^2), 2)
  nll <- 0
  for (rows in rows_by_stand) {
    Zj <- cbind(1, drought$precip10[rows])
    Vj <- Zj %*% G %*% t(Zj) + sigma^2 * diag(length(rows))
    nll <- nll - dmvnorm(drought$width[rows], as.vector(Zj %*% par[1:2]), Vj, log = TRUE)
  }
  nll
}
fit_rs_optim <- optim(c(0.9, 0.25, log(0.1), log(0.1), 0, log(0.1)), nll_rs, method = "BFGS")
```

```{r package-table}
tmb_sd <- attr(VarCorr(fit_rs_tmb)$cond$stand, "stddev")
lme_vc <- VarCorr(fit_rs_lme)
compare <- rbind(
  optim = c(fit_rs_optim$par[1:2], exp(fit_rs_optim$par[3:4]), tanh(fit_rs_optim$par[5]),
            exp(fit_rs_optim$par[6]), -fit_rs_optim$value),
  lmer = c(fixef(fit_rs_lmer), vc_rs, logLik(fit_rs_lmer)),
  lme = c(fixef(fit_rs_lme), as.numeric(lme_vc[1:2, "StdDev"]), as.numeric(lme_vc[2, "Corr"]),
          fit_rs_lme$sigma, logLik(fit_rs_lme)),
  glmmTMB = c(fixef(fit_rs_tmb)$cond, tmb_sd,
              attr(VarCorr(fit_rs_tmb)$cond$stand, "correlation")[1, 2],
              sigma(fit_rs_tmb), logLik(fit_rs_tmb)))
colnames(compare) <- c("mu_a", "mu_b", "tau_a", "tau_b", "rho", "sigma", "logLik")
round(compare, 4)
```

All four agree. The truth is $\mu_a = 0.9$, $\mu_b = 0.25$,
$\tau_a = 0.15$, $\tau_b = 0.10$, $\rho = -0.6$, $\sigma = 0.12$.

Which package when:

- **`glmmTMB`**: the most practical default. Many response distributions
  (negative binomial, beta, zero-inflated and hurdle models), unequal
  variances, and covariance structures such as `ar1()` and spatial
  `exp()`, all in one syntax. It writes the likelihood for you and uses
  automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation (see the
  [GLMM bonus](#glmm-by-hand)). Defaults to ML fits and Wald tests.
- **`lme4`** (`lmer()`, `glmer()`): better for inference on Normal
  models with few groups (REML fits, small-sample tests through
  `lmerTest`, profile intervals by default); fast with large crossed
  designs (stands and years). No correlation structures for the
  residuals.
- **`nlme`** (`lme()`, `gls()`): the richest set of residual correlation
  structures (`corAR1()`, spatial ones like `corExp()`) and unequal
  variances (`varIdent()`, `varPower()`) for Normal data. Normal
  responses only; crossed random effects are awkward.

The reference handout
[*Mixed models in R: nlme, lme4, and glmmTMB*](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf)
puts the three packages' syntax side by side, with advice on which to use.

## Discussion {#variance-discussion}

```{r four-stands, echo=FALSE}
short <- droplevels(drought[drought$stand %in% c("S09", "S10", "S11", "S12"), ])
fit_short <- lmer(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = short, REML = FALSE)
vc_short <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_short))$sdcor
```

**Q1.** Switching to AR(1) errors changed the trend's standard error
from `r f4(trend_ind[2])` to `r f4(se_ar1)` mm/yr, but the
precipitation slope's from `r f4(se_precip[1])` to `r f4(se_precip[2])`
mm/cm. Why would autocorrelated errors matter more for a trend over
time than for precipitation, which jumps around from year to year?

**Q2.** A colleague says: "I have only four stands, so I'll treat stand
as a fixed factor instead of a random intercept." Using the
random-intercept surface in [section 2](#harder), argue for or against.
What question is each model answering?

**Q3.** Fitting the random slope model to only the four short-record
stands (S09-S12, `r nrow(short)` stand-years) gives
$\hat\tau_a =$ `r f3(vc_short[1])`, $\hat\tau_b =$ `r f3(vc_short[2])`,
and $\hat\rho =$ `r f2(vc_short[3])`, with a "boundary (singular) fit"
message. Do these stands have perfectly correlated intercepts and
slopes? What would you report, and what would you change about the
model?

## Bonus: AR(1) by generalized least squares {#bonus-gls}

The [AR(1) fit](#ar1) searched over five parameters with `optim()`.
Matrix algebra cuts that to one. Write the covariance matrix as
$V = \sigma^2 R$, where $R_{st} = \rho^{|s-t|}/(1 - \rho^2)$ depends
only on $\rho$. If $\rho$ were known, the mean parameters and $\sigma^2$
that maximize the likelihood have closed forms:

$$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}(\rho) = (X^TR^{-1}X)^{-1}X^TR^{-1}\mathbf{y},
\qquad
\hat\sigma^2(\rho) = \frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{r}^TR^{-1}\mathbf{r},
\quad \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}(\rho)$$

This is **generalized least squares** (GLS). With $\rho = 0$, $R$ is
the identity matrix and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ reduces to the
ordinary [normal equations](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#least-squares),
$(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}$. With $\rho > 0$, $R^{-1}$ down-weights
information that neighboring years share.

Plugging $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}(\rho)$ and $\hat\sigma^2(\rho)$ back
into the likelihood leaves a function of $\rho$ alone (a profile
likelihood), which a one-dimensional search can maximize:

```{r gls-by-hand}
X_a <- cbind(1, chron_a$precip, chron_a$year_c)
y_a <- chron_a$width
n_a <- length(y_a)

gls_profile <- function(rho) {
  R <- rho^lags / (1 - rho^2)
  R_inv <- solve(R)
  beta <- solve(t(X_a) %*% R_inv %*% X_a, t(X_a) %*% R_inv %*% y_a)
  r <- as.vector(y_a - X_a %*% beta)
  sigma2 <- as.numeric(t(r) %*% R_inv %*% r) / n_a
  list(beta = as.vector(beta), sigma = sqrt(sigma2),
       loglik = dmvnorm(y_a, as.vector(X_a %*% beta), sigma2 * R, log = TRUE))
}
rho_gls <- optimize(function(rho) -gls_profile(rho)$loglik, c(-0.95, 0.95))$minimum
fit_by_hand <- gls_profile(rho_gls)
```

```{r gls-compare, echo=FALSE}
gls_tab <- rbind(
  "optim(), 5 parameters" = c(rho_hat, fit_ar1$par[1:3], exp(fit_ar1$par[5]), -fit_ar1$value),
  "GLS by hand, 1 parameter" = c(rho_gls, fit_by_hand$beta, fit_by_hand$sigma, fit_by_hand$loglik),
  "gls()" = c(coef(fit_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE), coef(fit_gls),
              fit_gls$sigma * sqrt(1 - coef(fit_gls$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)^2),
              logLik(fit_gls)))
colnames(gls_tab) <- c("rho", "a", "precip", "trend", "sigma", "logLik")
knitr::kable(gls_tab, digits = c(3, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3))
```

All three agree. `gls()` takes the same route: it profiles the mean
parameters and $\sigma$ out of the likelihood and searches only over
the correlation parameters. (It reports $\sigma$ as the SD of each
year's total error, $\sigma/\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$; the table converts it
back to the innovation SD.)

The profile also gives a likelihood interval for $\rho$:

```{r gls-profile-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.8}
rho_seq <- seq(-0.5, 0.9, by = 0.005)
ll_seq <- sapply(rho_seq, function(r) gls_profile(r)$loglik)
in_ci <- rho_seq[ll_seq > max(ll_seq) - 1.92]
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(rho_seq, ll_seq, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = expression(rho),
     ylab = "Profile log-likelihood")
abline(h = max(ll_seq) - 1.92, lty = 2)
abline(v = range(in_ci), lty = 3)
abline(v = rho_gls, col = "red")
```

The dashed line sits 1.92 below the maximum; the dotted lines mark the
approximate 95% interval for $\rho$, `r f2(min(in_ci))` to
`r f2(max(in_ci))`. Twenty-five years can't rule out $\rho = 0$, and
can't rule out the true value of 0.6 either.

## Bonus: a random intercept and AR(1) together {#bonus-combined}

The two structures combine. Using all four pinyon chronologies (100
stand-years), suppose each stand has its own random intercept and
AR(1) deviations within the stand:

$$\text{width}_{jt} = a + b_j + \beta\,\text{precip}_t + \eta_{jt},
\qquad b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_b^2),
\qquad \eta_{jt} = \rho\,\eta_{j,t-1} + \varepsilon_{jt}$$

$V$ is the sum of the two pieces: $\sigma_b^2$ wherever two values share
a stand, plus an AR(1) block within each stand. `kronecker(A, B)`
places a copy of `B` in every cell of `A`, scaled by that cell, so
`kronecker(diag(4), B)` makes a block-diagonal matrix with four copies
of `B`.

```{r combined-fit}
Z_chron <- model.matrix(~ 0 + stand, data = chron)
V_combined <- function(sigma_b, rho, sigma) {
  sigma_b^2 * Z_chron %*% t(Z_chron) + kronecker(diag(4), V_ar1(rho, sigma))
}
nll_combined <- function(par) {
  mu <- par[1] + par[2] * chron$precip
  V <- V_combined(exp(par[3]), tanh(par[4]), exp(par[5]))
  -dmvnorm(chron$width, mu, V, log = TRUE)
}
fit_comb <- optim(c(0.4, 0.02, log(0.1), 0, log(0.1)), nll_combined, method = "BFGS",
                  control = list(maxit = 1000))
c(a = fit_comb$par[1], b = fit_comb$par[2], sigma_b = exp(fit_comb$par[3]),
  rho = tanh(fit_comb$par[4]), sigma = exp(fit_comb$par[5]))

fit_lme <- lme(width ~ precip, random = ~ 1 | stand, data = chron,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ year | stand), method = "ML")
fixef(fit_lme)
coef(fit_lme$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
c(-fit_comb$value, logLik(fit_lme))       # same maximized log-likelihood
```

```{r combined-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4.5, fig.height=4.5}
show_matrix(V_combined(exp(fit_comb$par[3]), tanh(fit_comb$par[4]), exp(fit_comb$par[5])),
            main = "Fitted V (100 stand-years)")
```

Each block mixes the two structures: correlation decays with the lag
between years but levels off at the intraclass correlation instead of
reaching 0.

In matrix form, with a random slope as well:
$y = X\boldsymbol\beta + Zu + \eta$, with $u \sim \text{MVN}(0, G)$ as
in [random slopes](#random-slopes) and
$\eta \sim \text{MVN}(0, \sigma^2 R)$, where $R$ is the AR(1) matrix
from the [GLS bonus](#bonus-gls), block diagonal by stand. Then
$V = ZGZ^T + \sigma^2 R$: AR(1) errors replace $\sigma^2 I$ with
$\sigma^2 R$, and nothing else changes. The AR coefficient in $R$ and
the intercept-slope correlation in $G$ are different parameters, though
both are often written $\rho$. `glmmTMB` treats $\eta$ as one more
random effect with one level per observation, which is why its AR(1)
syntax drops the separate residual variance (`dispformula = ~0`; see the
[syntax handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf)).

## Bonus: a Poisson GLMM by hand {#glmm-by-hand}

For a count response the random effects can't be integrated out in
closed form (see
[integrating out a random effect](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#integrating)).
Suppose we counted cones on 8 trees in each of the 12 stands, with
tree vigor (standardized) as the predictor:

$$\text{cones}_{ij} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij}), \qquad
\log\lambda_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{vigor}_{ij} + b_j, \qquad
b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_b^2)$$

Each stand's likelihood is a one-dimensional integral over $b_j$, and
`integrate()` can do it numerically:

```{r glmm-by-hand}
set.seed(12)
cones <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, each = 8)),
                    vigor = round(rnorm(96), 2))
b_stand <- rnorm(12, 0, 0.5)
cones$count <- rpois(96, exp(1.5 + 0.4 * cones$vigor + b_stand[as.integer(cones$stand)]))

nll_glmm <- function(par) {
  sigma_b <- exp(par[3])
  nll <- 0
  for (g in split(cones, cones$stand)) {
    # integrand: P(this stand's counts | b) * density of b, for a vector of b values
    stand_lik <- function(b) {
      sapply(b, function(bi) exp(sum(dpois(g$count, exp(par[1] + par[2] * g$vigor + bi), log = TRUE)))) *
        dnorm(b, 0, sigma_b)
    }
    nll <- nll - log(integrate(stand_lik, -Inf, Inf)$value)
  }
  nll
}
fit_glmm <- optim(c(1, 0, log(0.3)), nll_glmm, method = "BFGS")
fit_glmm_tmb <- glmmTMB(count ~ vigor + (1 | stand), family = poisson, data = cones)

rbind(integrate = c(fit_glmm$par[1:2], exp(fit_glmm$par[3]), -fit_glmm$value),
      glmmTMB = c(fixef(fit_glmm_tmb)$cond, attr(VarCorr(fit_glmm_tmb)$cond$stand, "stddev"),
                  logLik(fit_glmm_tmb)))
```

The estimates agree to about two decimals; `glmmTMB`'s Laplace
approximation is close to the numerical integral here. A random
slope would make each stand's integral two-dimensional, and the cost of
grid-based integration grows with the number of grid points raised to
the number of random effects per group. That's why packages
approximate the integral, and why Bayesian samplers, which skip it, are
popular for complex hierarchical models. For other count and proportion
models (negative binomial, zero-inflated, binomial with trials) in
`lme4` and `glmmTMB`, see the
[mixed models handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_MixedModelSyntax.pdf).

# Bayesian hierarchical models {#bayesian-hierarchical}

The same random slope model, fit by MCMC. A Bayesian hierarchical model
puts priors on the population-level parameters (the among-stand SDs
and the correlation), and the sampler draws each stand's intercept and
slope along with everything else. This part covers partial pooling,
priors for a covariance matrix, the model written in Stan, and the same
model in one line of `brms`.

## 1. Random effects as priors

"Hierarchical," "multilevel," and "mixed" describe the same models. In
Bayesian terms, a random effect is a parameter whose prior has its own
unknown parameters (hyperparameters): each $(a_j, b_j)$ gets the prior
$\text{MVN}(0, G)$, and $G$ gets a prior too. Compared with fitting by
maximum likelihood:

- **No integral.** The sampler draws the $a_j$ and $b_j$ instead of
  integrating them out, so a Poisson or binomial response is no harder
  than a Normal one.
- **Uncertainty carries through.** Each stand's estimate reflects
  uncertainty in $\tau_a$, $\tau_b$, and $\rho$, rather than plugging in
  their best values.
- **Priors help with few groups.** A weakly informative prior keeps an
  SD off the boundary at 0 and a correlation off $\pm 1$, where
  maximum likelihood gave up in [Q3](#variance-discussion).
- **The price** is choosing priors and checking the sampler (see
  [checking chains](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks)).

## 2. Partial pooling {#partial-pooling}

There are three ways to estimate each stand's mean ring width:

- **complete pooling:** ignore stands; every stand gets the overall mean;
- **no pooling:** estimate each stand separately (stand as a fixed
  factor);
- **partial pooling:** the random effect, a compromise between the two.

Ignoring precipitation for the moment, a random intercept model gives
stand $j$ the estimate

$$\hat a_j = \hat\mu + w_j(\bar y_j - \hat\mu), \qquad
w_j = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2/n_j}$$

where $\bar y_j$ is the stand's own mean from $n_j$ years. The weight
$w_j$ compares the spread among stands ($\sigma_b^2$) with the sampling
variance of the stand's own mean ($\sigma^2/n_j$). A stand with a long
record keeps most of its own mean; a stand with 5 years is pulled
toward the overall mean. This is the same precision-weighted average as
a Normal prior combined with Normal data
([priors and posteriors](Week8_PosteriorsAndOptimization.html#priors)):
the population of stands acts as a prior for each stand.

```{r pooling-check}
fit_ri0 <- lmer(width ~ 1 + (1 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
sd_ri0 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_ri0))$sdcor          # sigma_b, sigma
ybar <- tapply(drought$width, drought$stand, mean)
n_j <- as.vector(table(drought$stand))
w <- sd_ri0[1]^2 / (sd_ri0[1]^2 + sd_ri0[2]^2 / n_j)
round(cbind(own_mean = ybar, n_j, w, formula = fixef(fit_ri0) + w * (ybar - fixef(fit_ri0)),
            lmer = coef(fit_ri0)$stand[, 1]), 3)
```

The formula matches `lmer()`'s stand estimates. Here
$\hat\sigma_b =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[1])` and $\hat\sigma =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[2])`;
the widget starts at those values. It plots each stand's own mean and
its partially pooled estimate.

```{r widget-pooling, echo=FALSE}
widget("partial_pooling.html")
```

> **Question:** Set $\sigma_b$ to 0, then drag it to 0.4. Which two
> pooling choices are these? Then compare S10 and S12: their own means
> are similar (`r f2(ybar["S10"])` and `r f2(ybar["S12"])`), but one has
> 8 years and the other 5. Which moves more toward the overall mean, and
> why?

## 3. Priors for a covariance matrix {#lkj}

The random slope model needs a prior on $G$, a 2 $\times$ 2 covariance
matrix. The usual approach splits $G$ into scales and correlations,

$$G = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_a & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_b \end{pmatrix}
\Omega
\begin{pmatrix} \tau_a & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_b \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Omega = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

and puts separate priors on each piece: a half-Normal, half-$t$, or
exponential prior on each SD $\tau$, and an **LKJ prior** on the
correlation matrix $\Omega$ (named for Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe).
Older BUGS and JAGS code often used an inverse-Wishart prior on $G$
instead, which ties the prior on the SDs to the prior on the
correlations; splitting them makes each easier to choose.

The LKJ density has one shape parameter $\eta$:

$$p(\Omega) \propto \det(\Omega)^{\eta - 1}$$

For a 2 $\times$ 2 matrix, $\det(\Omega) = 1 - \rho^2$, so
$p(\rho) \propto (1 - \rho^2)^{\eta - 1}$. With $\eta = 1$ every
correlation is equally likely; $\eta > 1$ favors correlations near 0,
and $\eta < 1$ favors correlations near $\pm 1$. For a bigger matrix
($K \times K$), each single correlation has the marginal prior
$(\rho + 1)/2 \sim \text{Beta}(\eta - 1 + K/2,\ \eta - 1 + K/2)$.

```{r widget-lkj, echo=FALSE}
widget("lkj_prior.html")
```

> **Question:** For a 10 $\times$ 10 correlation matrix with $\eta = 1$,
> how likely is any one correlation to exceed 0.5 in absolute value?
> What does "uniform" mean for a matrix that large?

## 4. Random slopes in Stan {#stan-model}

The Stan program below is the random slope model with an LKJ(2) prior
on $\Omega$. Two choices in it need explaining.

- **The Cholesky factor.** Stan works with $L$, the lower-triangular
  matrix with $LL^T = \Omega$. Any value Stan proposes for
  `cholesky_factor_corr` gives a valid correlation matrix, so the
  sampler can't leave the allowed region (the third problem in
  [why these models are harder to fit](#harder)), and it's cheaper to
  compute with.
- **Non-centered stand effects.** Instead of sampling $(a_j, b_j)$
  directly, Stan samples standard Normal $z_j$ and computes
  $(a_j, b_j)^T = \text{diag}(\tau)\,L\,z_j$. This avoids the funnel
  that makes hierarchical models hard to sample
  ([when HMC struggles](Week9_MCMC.html#hmc-failures)).

```{r stan-fit, cache=TRUE, echo=-6, results="hide"}
library(cmdstanr)
slopes_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;                       // stand-years
  int<lower=1> J;                       // stands
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=J> stand;
  vector[N] x;                          // precipitation (10 cm, centered at 20 cm)
  vector[N] y;                          // ring width (mm)
}
parameters {
  vector[2] mu;                         // mean intercept and slope
  vector<lower=0>[2] tau;               // among-stand SDs of intercepts and slopes
  cholesky_factor_corr[2] L;            // Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix
  matrix[2, J] z;                       // standardized stand effects
  real<lower=0> sigma;                  // residual SD
}
transformed parameters {
  // row j: stand j's intercept and slope
  matrix[J, 2] ab = rep_matrix(mu', J) + (diag_pre_multiply(tau, L) * z)';
}
model {
  mu[1] ~ normal(1, 0.5);
  mu[2] ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  tau ~ normal(0, 0.3);                 // half-normal, because tau > 0
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(z) ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ normal(0, 0.3);
  y ~ normal(ab[stand, 1] + ab[stand, 2] .* x, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real rho = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L)[1, 2];
}
"
slopes_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(slopes_code))
stan_data <- list(N = nrow(drought), J = 12, stand = as.integer(drought$stand),
                  x = drought$precip10, y = drought$width)
fit_stan <- slopes_model$sample(data = stan_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4,
                                seed = 746, refresh = 0)
fit_stan$draws()
```

Check the sampler first, then the estimates:

```{r stan-check}
fit_stan$diagnostic_summary()
fit_stan$summary(c("mu", "tau", "rho", "sigma"))
```

```{r stan-numbers, echo=FALSE}
library(posterior)
draws <- as_draws_df(fit_stan$draws(c("mu", "tau", "rho", "sigma", "ab")))
q <- function(v) quantile(v, c(0.5, 0.05, 0.95))
post <- rbind(mu_a = q(draws$`mu[1]`), mu_b = q(draws$`mu[2]`), tau_a = q(draws$`tau[1]`),
              tau_b = q(draws$`tau[2]`), rho = q(draws$rho), sigma = q(draws$sigma))
ml_vs_bayes <- data.frame(truth = c(0.9, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, -0.6, 0.12),
                          lmer = compare["lmer", 1:6], post)
names(ml_vs_bayes)[3:5] <- c("posterior median", "5%", "95%")
ab_post <- cbind(sapply(1:12, function(s) mean(draws[[sprintf("ab[%d,1]", s)]])),
                 sapply(1:12, function(s) mean(draws[[sprintf("ab[%d,2]", s)]])))
err <- function(est, rows = 1:12) colMeans(abs(est[rows, ] - ab_true[rows, ]))
err_nopool <- err(nopool)
err_post <- err(ab_post)
short_rows <- which(n_years <= 8)
err_nopool_short <- err(nopool, short_rows)
err_post_short <- err(ab_post, short_rows)
```

```{r ml-bayes-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(ml_vs_bayes, digits = 3, caption = "Maximum likelihood (lmer) and posterior summaries")
```

The two methods agree closely on everything except the correlation: the
MLE is `r f2(compare["lmer", "rho"])`, while the posterior median is
`r f2(post["rho", 1])` with a 90% interval from `r f2(post["rho", 2])`
to `r f2(post["rho", 3])`.

```{r rho-posterior, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
hist(draws$rho, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white", xlim = c(-1, 1),
     main = "", xlab = expression(rho ~ "(intercept-slope correlation)"))
curve(dbeta((x + 1) / 2, 2, 2) / 2, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = compare["lmer", "rho"], lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = -0.6, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("LKJ(2) prior", "MLE (lmer)", "truth"), lty = c(2, 1, 3), lwd = 2,
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

```{r shrinkage-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(nopool, pch = 1, cex = 1.2, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)",
     xlim = range(nopool[, 1], ab_post[, 1]) + c(0, 0.06), ylim = range(nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 2]))
arrows(nopool[, 1], nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 1], ab_post[, 2], length = 0.07, col = "steelblue")
points(ab_post, pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
text(nopool, labels = paste0(stand_names, " (", n_years, ")"), pos = 4, cex = 0.65, col = "grey40")
points(post["mu_a", 1], post["mu_b", 1], pch = 3, cex = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("own least-squares fit", "posterior mean", "population mean"),
       pch = c(1, 19, 3), col = c("black", "steelblue", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

Each arrow runs from a stand's own fit to its posterior mean; the
number in parentheses is the record length. Stands with short records
move the most; stands with 24 or 30 years barely move.

```{r shrink-sims, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(746)
shrink_sims <- t(replicate(500, {
  ab <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)
  sim <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)))
  k <- as.integer(sim$stand)
  sim$x <- (round(rgamma(nrow(sim), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1) - 20) / 10
  sim$y <- ab[k, 1] + ab[k, 2] * sim$x + rnorm(nrow(sim), 0, 0.12)
  np <- t(sapply(split(sim, sim$stand), function(s) coef(lm(y ~ x, data = s))))
  pp <- as.matrix(coef(lmer(y ~ x + (x | stand), data = sim, REML = FALSE))$stand)
  sh <- n_years <= 8
  c(np_a = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 1]), np_b = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 2]),
    pp_a = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 1]), pp_b = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 2]))
}))
```

Because the data are simulated, we can compare both sets of estimates
with the true stand values. For the four stands with 5 or 8 years, the
average error in the slopes is `r f3(err_nopool_short[2])` mm per 10 cm
with no pooling and `r f3(err_post_short[2])` with partial pooling
(intercepts: `r f3(err_nopool_short[1])` and `r f3(err_post_short[1])`
mm). That's a mixed result: in any one data set, shrinkage can pull a
stand that really is unusual too far toward the mean. Its advantage is
on average. Over `r nrow(shrink_sims)` simulated data sets with the same
design, using `lmer()`'s stand estimates, partial pooling cut the
average slope error for the short-record stands from
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_b"]))` to `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_b"]))`
(intercepts: `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_a"]))` to
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_a"]))`).

> **Question:** Why is the posterior for $\rho$ so much wider than the
> other posteriors, and why is its median closer to 0 than the MLE?
> Which summary is more honest about what 12 stands can tell us?

> **Question:** Change `lkj_corr_cholesky(2)` to `lkj_corr_cholesky(1)`,
> then to `lkj_corr_cholesky(10)`, and refit. Predict how the posterior
> for $\rho$ will move before you run each one. Do the stand estimates
> change much?

## 5. The same model in brms {#brms}

`brms` writes the Stan program from a `lme4`-style formula. Here are
the same model and priors (the fixed-effect priors are left at `brms`'s
defaults):

```{r brms-fit, cache=TRUE, results="hide"}
library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought,
                prior = c(prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sd),
                          prior(lkj(2), class = cor),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sigma)),
                backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0)
```

```{r brms-summary}
summary(fit_brms)
```

The estimates match the hand-written model up to Monte Carlo error.
`stancode(fit_brms)` prints the Stan program `brms` wrote; it uses the
same Cholesky factor and non-centered stand effects. Without the
`prior` argument, `brms` uses an LKJ(1) prior on the correlations and
half-Student-$t$ priors on the SDs; `prior_summary(fit_brms)` lists
every prior in a fit. `rstanarm::stan_lmer()` fits the same formula
from precompiled models, so it skips the compile step.

## Discussion {#bayes-discussion}

**Q1.** With 12 stands, the 90% interval for $\rho$ runs from
`r f2(post["rho", 2])` to `r f2(post["rho", 3])`. To rule out
$\rho = 0$, would you rather have 12 more stands or 20 more years at
each of the 12 stands? Defend your choice.

**Q2.** When would you use `brms`, and when would you write the Stan
model yourself?

**Q3.** Do your final project data have groups (sites, individuals,
years, observers)? Which effects would you treat as random, and would
you let any slopes vary among groups?

## Bonus: ridge regression as a prior {#ridge-prior}

A [ridge penalty](Week10_ModelComparison.html#regularization) adds
$\lambda\sum\beta_k^2$ to the NLL. A Normal(0, $\tau^2$) prior on each
$\beta_k$ adds $-\log p(\beta) = \sum\beta_k^2/(2\tau^2)$ plus a
constant, which is the same penalty with $\lambda = 1/(2\tau^2)$; a
Laplace prior gives the lasso (see
[Bayesian model comparison and shrinkage priors](Week10_ModelComparison.html#bayesian)).
A random effect does the same thing to the stand deviations: the
$\text{MVN}(0, G)$ prior shrinks every $(a_j, b_j)$ toward 0. The
difference is that $\tau$ isn't chosen by cross-validation; it's
estimated from how much the stands actually differ.
